excerpt: The NCERT Class 6 chapter Playing with Numbers packs factors, multiples, primes, divisibility rules and HCF & LCM into one place. Here is how the ideas connect, with two worked case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Class 6 student what a factor is and you will often hear ‘a number that divides’ — which is right, but half-remembered. The NCERT chapter Playing with Numbers is where Class 6 maths factors and multiples finally click into a single, connected picture: factors and multiples are two sides of the same coin, primes are the building blocks, divisibility rules are shortcuts, and HCF & LCM are what you actually reach for in word problems. Get this chapter right and Class 7 fractions feel almost easy.

I have taught this chapter to Tier-2 city students who could recite the rules but froze on a two-line word problem. The fix is never more rules — it is seeing how the pieces fit. So let us walk the chapter the way the ideas depend on each other, then solve two real case studies at the end.

Factors and multiples: the same relationship, two directions

A factor of a number divides it exactly, leaving no remainder. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. A multiple is what you get by multiplying: 12, 24, 36 and 48 are all multiples of 12. Notice the symmetry — if 3 is a factor of 12, then 12 is a multiple of 3. Same fact, read from two ends.

Two things worth burning into memory: 1 is a factor of every number, and every number is a factor (and a multiple) of itself. Also, factors are finite but multiples never stop — you can always multiply by one more.

Prime and composite numbers

A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. So 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 are prime. A composite number has more than two factors, like 4, 6, 9 and 12. Here is the part students forget: 1 is neither prime nor composite — it has only one factor. And 2 is the only even prime, which throws people every time.

Divisibility rules — the shortcuts that save exam minutes

Divisibility rules let you test a factor without doing the full division. In the exam, they turn a 30-second sum into a 3-second glance. These are the rules NCERT expects in Class 6.

Divisible byRuleQuick example
2Last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 834 → yes
3Sum of digits is divisible by 381 → 8+1=9 → yes
4Last two digits form a number divisible by 4316 → yes
5Last digit is 0 or 5245 → yes
6Divisible by both 2 and 372 → even and 7+2=9 → yes
9Sum of digits is divisible by 9729 → 7+2+9=18 → yes
10Last digit is 0560 → yes
11Difference of alternate digit sums is 0 or a multiple of 11121 → (1+1)−2=0 → yes

The rule for 11 is the one everyone finds fiddly, so here it is slowly: add the digits in odd places, add the digits in even places, and subtract. If the answer is 0 or a multiple of 11, the number is divisible by 11.

Prime factorisation: writing a number as a product of primes

Every composite number can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way — this is the idea behind prime factorisation. Take 60: keep dividing by the smallest prime that works. 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. So 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. The factor tree and the repeated-division ladder both land in the same place; use whichever you find clearer.

HCF and LCM: where the chapter earns its keep

The Highest Common Factor (HCF) is the biggest number that divides two or more numbers. The Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest number they all divide into. Prime factorisation makes both painless:

  • HCF — multiply the primes the numbers share, taking the lowest power of each.
  • LCM — multiply every prime that appears, taking the highest power of each.
  • Handy check — for any two numbers, HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.

One counter-intuitive point I always stress: HCF is never bigger than the smaller number, and LCM is never smaller than the bigger number. If a student’s answer breaks that, it is wrong before you check anything else.

Case study 1: packing sweet boxes (HCF)

Read the passage. A shopkeeper in Jaipur has 24 kaju katli and 36 barfi. He wants to pack them into identical boxes so that each box has only one kind of sweet and every box holds the same number of sweets, with none left over. What is the largest number of sweets he can put in each box, and how many boxes will he need?

Solution. ‘Largest number that divides both’ means HCF. 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Shared primes at lowest power: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. So each box holds 12 sweets. Boxes needed: 24 ÷ 12 = 2 boxes of kaju katli and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 boxes of barfi — 5 boxes in all.

Case study 2: traffic lights blinking together (LCM)

Two traffic signals at a crossing blink at intervals of 48 seconds and 72 seconds. They blink together at 8:00 am sharp. When will they next blink together?

Solution. ‘Next time both events line up’ means LCM. 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Take the highest power of each prime: 2⁴ × 3² = 16 × 9 = 144. So they blink together every 144 seconds, that is 2 minutes 24 seconds later — at 8:02:24 am.

questions.q: What is the prime factorisation of 60?
questions.explanation: Only 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 uses primes throughout. The others still contain composite numbers.

questions.q: What is the HCF of 24 and 36?
questions.explanation: 24 = 2×2×2×3 and 36 = 2×2×3×3. Shared primes at lowest power: 2×2×3 = 12.

questions.q: What is the LCM of 8 and 12?
Which number is neither prime nor composite?
questions.explanation: 1 has exactly one factor, itself, so it is neither prime nor composite.
For 132, alternate digit sums are (1+2)=3 and 3; the difference 3−3=0, which is a multiple of 11.

faq.q: What is the difference between a factor and a multiple?
faq.a: A factor divides a number exactly with no remainder, while a multiple is the result of multiplying that number. For 12, the factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, but its multiples are 12, 24, 36 and so on without end.

faq.q: Is 1 a prime number in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: No. A prime number needs exactly two different factors, but 1 has only one factor — itself. So 1 is neither prime nor composite, and the smallest prime is 2.

faq.q: When should I use HCF and when LCM in a word problem?
faq.a: Use HCF when you are splitting or grouping into the largest equal parts with nothing left over. Use LCM when you are looking for the first time repeating events line up again, like bells or lights blinking together.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to check divisibility by 3 and 9?
faq.a: Add up all the digits. If that sum is divisible by 3, the number is too; if the sum is divisible by 9, the number is divisible by 9. For 729, the digits add to 18, which works for both.
